title: The princes of Samarkand
summary:
The following article appeared in the Thüringer Allgemeine on 1 October 2026. Reproduced with kind permission.

The princes of Samarkand

There is a Thuringian story behind Germany's bronze medal at the Chess Olympiad. It is a story of youth development that began two decades ago - and is closely linked to national coach Bernd Vökler from Apolda.

When Rasmus Svane sits down to dinner in Bad Blankenburg a few weeks before the Chess Olympiad, the medal in Samarkand is still a distant dream. The national team players are preparing for the highlight of the season at the regional sports school - supported by grandmaster Peter Svidler, once a second to former world champion Vladimir Kramnik and a commentator for the official YouTube channel at the Olympiad. After a long day of training, Svane jokes that if they manage to win a medal in Uzbekistan, it will surely be thanks to the excellent raspberry spritzer in Bad Blankenburg.

They do. Germany wins bronze - the first medal for a German men's team at a Chess Olympiad in 26 years. The joke about the spritzer becomes a symbol. For many of the paths leading to this success do indeed point to Thuringia.

Above all, they lead to Bernd Vökler. The Apolda native has been Germany's national youth coach since 2003 and has since become one of the most important sources of ideas within the German Chess Federation. Anyone who wants to understand why the current generation is so successful has to look back two decades.

In 2008, the Chess Olympiad is held in Dresden. As the host nation, Germany is allowed to enter three teams - and Vökler uses the opportunity for an experiment. Instead of filling another team with experienced masters, he sends a youth squad into the competition. The young players perform surprisingly well against international opposition.

A year later, Vökler goes a step further. At the time, intensive support in Germany generally begins only at the age of 14 or 15. He wants to start earlier and brings nine- and ten-year-olds into a five-year development programme. The group known as the Chess Princes is born.

Matthias Blübaum, Alexander Donchenko and Rasmus Svane are among them. Seventeen years later, all three are part of Germany's bronze-medal team in Samarkand - together with Vincent Keymer and Frederik Svane, who are six years younger. The Chess Princes of the past have become medal winners.

But early development alone is not enough for Vökler. With the "Chess Year", he gives young elite players the opportunity to spend a year between school and university treating chess as a profession. Blübaum is among the first to try it.

While the national team players are fighting for bronze in Uzbekistan, Vökler is already back in Bad Blankenburg training the next group of young players. When the medal is confirmed, he sends a group photograph of the youngsters to Samarkand. The young princes send their greetings to the crown princes.

Vincent Keymer, Matthias Blübaum, Frederik Svane and Rasmus Svane representing Germany in their round-ten match against France in Samarkand (a 3-1 victory with wins by the Svane brothers on the bottom boards) | Photo: Rafal Oleksiewicz / FIDE

There is also a historical link to Thuringia. When Germany won silver in Istanbul in 2000, its most recent medal until now, grandmaster Thomas Luther was one of the players at the board. Twenty-six years later, he is there again. As head of the relevant FIDE commission, the Erfurt-born grandmaster oversees the Para Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, held alongside the main Olympiad for the first time. At the same time, he watches a new German generation reach the podium - with players, some of whom had not even been born when he helped win silver.

The latest success is likely to have an impact far beyond the sporting result. The Olympiad counts as a so-called target event for German federal funding. Finishing among the world's top three could improve chess' ranking and bring in additional funding of around 120,000 euros per year.

And the next talents are already sitting at the board. Among the most promising is 14-year-old Christian Glöckler. He was discovered and guided to the top by Erfurt grandmaster Thomas Pähtz, who was part of East Germany's Olympiad team in 1988. Vökler, meanwhile, is driving Germany's bid to host the 2028 World Junior Championship in Bad Blankenburg. If the bid succeeds, talents such as Glöckler could be given a major stage in front of a home crowd.

The bronze medal therefore tells a story not only of five grandmasters and two remarkable weeks in Uzbekistan. It also tells of decisions taken when some of these players were still children. And of youth development whose rewards in chess often become visible only several moves later.

Many people played a part in the success in Samarkand. But an important part of its story begins in Thuringia - with Bernd Vökler's bold idea. And, Rasmus Svane might add, a little with the raspberry spritzer from Bad Blankenburg.

title: Nakamura Sets New Chess.com Rating Record As Artemiev Pulls Out Last-Second Win
summary: A day after becoming the first 3500-rated Chess.com Blitz player in site history, GM Hikaru Nakamura upped his record to 3503 while streaming Titled Tuesday live from Sithonia, Greece, on October 6. Unfortunately for Nakamura, he did not ultimately win the tournament, an honor which went to GM Vladislav Artemiev after he defeated Nakamura in the final round. Titled Tuesday ft. the highest-rated blitz player ever 🐐 @GMHikaru https://t.co/UYVbs2frlJ In case you missed it, here's this week's broadcast live from Greece: Nakamura had reached exactly 3500 before the event, explaining to Chess.com's Tarjei Svensen, "Unless I'm only going to skip [Titled Tuesday and 3 0 Thursday] every week, there's no way even to keep my rating where it is... I view this as very much a one-time thing and that's also why I made it a big point to go for it yesterday." That's not a typo - Hikaru hits 3500! 👏 https://t.co/ZEJ3EPUCEO "My goal in Titled Tuesday [is] like every Titled Tuesday," he also indicated, meaning victory. "First and foremost, because there are actually people watching [in person], I'd like to be competitive where I'm not losing a bunch of games early. That's the starting point." Nakamura achieved that goal, starting with two self described smooth games, but a draw in the fourth round kept him off the roll of perfect players entering the first break in play. Artemiev was among the 17 who did make 4/4, a list which also included last week's victor GM Wesley So as well as GMs Sina Movahed, Alexey Sarana, Awonder Liang, and Liem Le, among others. As usual, the list of perfect players quickly dwindled exiting the break. Artemiev and So lost to Movahed and Liang in round five, and by the end of round six, just three remained perfect: Le, Sarana, and FM Dincer Tasdogen. A round farther in, that list was down to one. Nakamura contributed by defeating Sarana out of a theoretically drawn opening that Sarana either didn't know or remember, or chose not to pursue.
